method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Urticaria' (Last updated March 2023), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: **Most urticaria is idiopathic or viral**; viral infection is a common cause in children, during or after the illness.
claims.source_text: There are many causes for urticaria, most are idiopathic or viral … Viral infection is a common cause of urticaria in children … Urticaria may occur both during and after an illness when the child is otherwise well
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Urticaria' (Last updated March 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Urticaria/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Urticaria with airway, respiratory, cardiovascular or gastrointestinal involvement: suspect anaphylaxis — urgent adrenaline and medical assessment.**
claims.source_text: If urticaria occurs with involvement of other systems (eg airway, respiratory, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal), anaphylaxis should be suspected. Urgent administration of adrenaline and medical assessment is required
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Urticaria' (Last updated March 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Urticaria/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Acute: under 6 weeks. Chronic: most days for more than 6 weeks** — usually idiopathic, sometimes inducible or autoimmune.
claims.source_text: Acute urticaria lasts for less than 6 weeks and chronic urticaria occurs most days for more than 6 weeks … Chronic urticaria (>6 weeks) is usually idiopathic, but can also be inducible (associated with a physical trigger) or autoimmune-related
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Urticaria' (Last updated March 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Urticaria/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Suspect allergy when episodes are rare, short-lived and circumstantial**: only with exercise, always within 1–2 hours of a meal, or with abdominal pain, vomiting, breathing difficulty or dizziness.
claims.source_text: Suspect if episodes are rare, short-lived and occur under specific circumstances: Only when exercising Always within 1-2 hours of a meal When other symptoms occur around the same time such as abdominal pain, vomiting, breathing difficulty or dizziness
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Urticaria' (Last updated March 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Urticaria/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Allergic urticaria appears within 1–2 hours of exposure and fades within 6–8 hours. Urticaria lasting days is almost never allergy** (except some medication allergies).
claims.source_text: Urticaria usually appears within 1-2 hours of the exposure and disappears within 6-8 hours … Urticaria lasting days are almost never due to allergy (with the exception of some medication allergies)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Urticaria' (Last updated March 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Urticaria/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Urticaria during an antibiotic course is often the infection, not antibiotic allergy.** Take a detailed drug allergy history; consider drug allergy clinic referral.
claims.source_text: Urticaria occurring at the time of antibiotic use is often due to the underlying infection rather than an allergy to the antibiotic. Take a detailed drug allergy history and consider specialist drug allergy clinic referral
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Urticaria' (Last updated March 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Urticaria/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Wheals are well circumscribed, often coalescent, usually gone within 24 hours, and migrate** from site to site within minutes to hours.
claims.source_text: Well circumscribed but often coalescent May appear within minutes and usually resolve within 24 hours Transient and appear to “migrate”, disappearing within minutes to hours from one location and reappearing elsewhere
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Urticaria' (Last updated March 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Urticaria/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Angioedema** is larger, painful rather than itchy, and may take up to 72 hours to resolve.
claims.source_text: Compared to wheals, the swollen lesions are larger, may be painful or uncomfortable rather than pruritic, and may last longer taking up to 72 hours to resolve
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Urticaria' (Last updated March 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Urticaria/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Urticaria: non-target lesions with central pallor. Erythema multiforme: target lesions with central purpura.**
claims.source_text: Urticaria: non-target lesions (central pallor) … Erythema multiforme: target lesion (central purpura)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Urticaria' (Last updated March 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Urticaria/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Urticarial vasculitis (including HSP):** painful, lasts over 48 hours, leaves discolouration.
claims.source_text: Urticarial vasculitis (including HSP): lesions are usually painful rather than pruritic, last >48 hours and leave discolouration on the skin
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Urticaria' (Last updated March 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Urticaria/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Recurrent angioedema without wheals: think C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency** — urticaria is not a feature of it.
claims.source_text: Urticaria is not a feature of C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency. If recurrent angioedema without wheals, think of C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Urticaria' (Last updated March 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Urticaria/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Investigations are almost never indicated for acute urticaria; routine allergy tests are not required** (a common misconception worth discussing). They may be indicated in chronic urticaria with features of an underlying cause.
claims.source_text: Investigations Almost never indicated for acute urticaria … Routine allergy tests are generally not required. This is a common misconception and may require discussion with the family … May be indicated for chronic urticaria if there are features suggestive of an underlying cause
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Urticaria' (Last updated March 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Urticaria/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Most acute cases resolve untreated in days to weeks.** Remove triggers, avoid heat and spicy food, **avoid NSAIDs**, use a cool compress.
claims.source_text: Most cases only last for a few days or weeks and resolve without any treatment Remove identifiable triggers Avoid aggravating factors (eg excessive heat or spicy foods) Avoid NSAIDs as they often make symptoms worse Cool compress
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Urticaria' (Last updated March 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Urticaria/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Non-sedating antihistamine, e.g. cetirizine orally:** 6–11 months 0.25 mg/kg (max 2.5 mg) daily · 1–2 years 2.5 mg twice daily · 2–6 years 5 mg daily or 2.5 mg twice daily · 6–12 years 10 mg daily or 5 mg twice daily · 12–18 years 10 mg daily.
claims.source_text: Non-sedating formulation is preferred Eg cetirizine 6-11 months: 0.25 mg/kg (max 2.5 mg) oral daily 1-2 years: 2.5 mg oral twice daily 2-6 years: 5 mg oral daily or 2.5 mg oral twice daily 6-12 years: 10 mg oral daily or 5 mg oral twice daily 12-18 years: 10 mg oral daily
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Urticaria' (Last updated March 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Urticaria/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Severe and not responding to antihistamines:** consider a single dose of prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg (max 60 mg) orally. **Steroid creams are not effective.**
claims.source_text: A single dose of oral prednisolone 0.5-1 mg/kg (max 60 mg) may be considered in severe cases not responding to antihistamines … Steroid creams are not effective
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Urticaria' (Last updated March 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Urticaria/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Chronic urticaria:** start as for acute; if ongoing, **cetirizine can go up to 4 times the recommended daily dose** (6 years and older: max 40 mg total daily), and a sedating antihistamine may be added. Still persisting: specialist advice; immunomodulators only with an allergy specialist.
claims.source_text: Initial treatment is the same as for acute urticaria … Cetirizine dose can be increased up to 4 times the recommended daily dose. Eg in children 6 years and older, cetirizine maximum total daily dose of 40mg … A sedating antihistamine may be added … If symptoms persist, seek specialist advice. Immunomodulator therapy may be considered in consultation with allergy specialist
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Urticaria' (Last updated March 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Urticaria/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Discuss with the paediatric team:** fever, bruising, joint pain or systemic features · anaphylaxis · angioedema · age under 6 months · chronic urticaria over 6 weeks.
claims.source_text: Consider consultation with local paediatric team when Associated fever, bruising, joint pain or other or systemic features (need to exclude urticarial vasculitis or chronic urticaria as a manifestation of another disease process) Anaphylaxis Angioedema Age <6 months Chronic urticaria (>6 weeks)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Urticaria' (Last updated March 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Urticaria/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Discharge once anaphylaxis is excluded — most children do not need admission.**
claims.source_text: Consider discharge when Anaphylaxis has been excluded Most patients do not need admission for urticaria
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Urticaria' (Last updated March 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Urticaria/, retrieved 2026-09-23
